slides.0.subtitle: Horse Heaven Hills, Wahluke Slope, Ancient Lakes and Puget Sound
slides.1.title: Horse Heaven Hills and the Wahluke Slope
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Horse Heaven Hills
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Approved 1 July 2005, about 570,000 acres; very windy (about 30% more wind run than Walla Walla and Yakima); about 6.2 inches of rain a year
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Wahluke Slope
slides.1.highlights.1.content: About 81,000 acres with about 8,932 planted, nearly 15% of the state's winegrape acreage; about 5.9 inches of rain and about 3,013 degree days; deep windblown sand and loess (approved late 2005 or 2006, sources differ)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Varieties
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Horse Heaven Hills lists 16 varieties including Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache and Riesling; Wahluke Slope is known mainly for Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon
slides.1.content: Both are dry, warm sub-regions of the Columbia Valley: one windy, one very warm.
slides.2.title: Ancient Lakes and the other AVAs
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Ancient Lakes
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Approved 18 October 2012 (HistoryLink says 2013); about 162,762 acres with 1,604 planted; mostly at 1,200 to 1,500 feet, and mainly white varieties such as Riesling and Chardonnay
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Puget Sound
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Approved 4 October 1995; 17 to 60 inches of rain a year; suited to cool varieties such as Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe and Müller-Thurgau; most wineries use grapes from eastern Washington
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Newer AVAs
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Lake Chelan (2009), Snipes Mountain (2009), Naches Heights (2011), Lewis-Clark Valley (2016, mostly in Idaho) and Candy Mountain (2020)
slides.2.content: Washington's AVAs are mostly in the dry east, with Puget Sound the one wet and cool exception.
slides.3.title: Walla Walla's winery story
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Variety mix (2007)
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Cabernet Sauvignon about 41%, Merlot about 26% and Syrah about 16% (2007 data; the picture has changed since)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Climate
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A 190–220 day growing season and about 3,024 degree days; big day–night swings, with cold air from the Blue Mountains causing sudden changes and winter lows reaching −20°F
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Soils
slides.3.content: Walla Walla's pioneers were covered in L1; climatically, winter cold is the main risk.
